verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE OPINION — PROVISION AND USE OF WORK EQUIPMENT REGULATIONS 1998 AND A DISTRIBUTOR SUPPLYING BY WAY OF SALE
Position stated as at 2026-11-21 (Great Britain)

=====================================================================
1. ANSWER IN ONE LINE
=====================================================================
No. The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 do not apply to a person in respect of work equipment supplied by that person by way of sale, agreement for sale or hire-purchase agreement. That is the express effect of regulation 3(5), the final limb of the scope clause. A distributor is not a PUWER duty holder in respect of the sale itself.

=====================================================================
2. BASIS ON WHICH THIS OPINION IS GIVEN (state these on the face of the advice)
=====================================================================
(a) JURISDICTION — GREAT BRITAIN. The request does not name a jurisdiction. Great Britain and Northern Ireland each have an instrument called the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998, and their texts differ. This opinion is given on the Great Britain instrument, SI 1998/2306, which is the instrument covered by the sources used (legislation.gov.uk and HSE). If the distributor operates in Northern Ireland the relevant instrument is the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1998 (SR 1998/279), enforced by HSENI; the equivalent sale exclusion is expected to be in the same terms but has NOT been verified against the sources available for this opinion and must be re-checked before reliance.

(b) CAPACITY OF THE DISTRIBUTOR. The opinion assumes the distributor's only relevant connection with the equipment is that it sold it. It assumes the distributor is not, in relation to the same equipment, (i) an employer providing it for use by its own employees, (ii) a relevant self-employed person using it at work, or (iii) a person having control of it, of a person using it, or of the way it is used, at the purchaser's premises. Where any of those is true, PUWER can attach on that separate basis — see section 6.

(c) MEANING OF 'THE SCOPE CLAUSE'. Regulation 3 (headed 'Application') of PUWER 1998 — the provision that fixes where the Regulations apply, to whom the requirements are addressed, and the sale/hire-purchase carve-out.

(d) VERSION. The text relied on is the latest revised text carried on legislation.gov.uk, fetched 2026-11-23T00:07:02Z, which carries the banner 'There are currently no known outstanding effects for The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998'. It is cross-checked against the 2013-07-01 point-in-time version and against HSE L22 (Fourth edition, 2014). See section 8 for the full currency record and its residual limitation.

=====================================================================
3. THE SCOPE CLAUSE — VERBATIM TEXT (regulation 3, GB, as currently in force)
=====================================================================

Regulation 3 — Application

(1) These Regulations shall apply—
    (a) in Great Britain; and
    (b) outside Great Britain as sections 1 to 59 and 80 to 82 of the 1974 Act apply by virtue of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 (Application outside Great Britain) Order 1995 ('the 1995 Order').

(2) The requirements imposed by these Regulations on an employer in respect of work equipment shall apply to such equipment provided for use or used by an employee of his at work.

(3) The requirements imposed by these Regulations on an employer shall also apply—
    (a) to a [relevant self-employed person], in respect of work equipment he uses at work;
    (b) subject to paragraph (5), to a person who has control to any extent of—
        (i) work equipment;
        (ii) a person at work who uses or supervises or manages the use of work equipment; or
        (iii) the way in which work equipment is used at work,
        and to the extent of his control.

(4) Any reference in paragraph (3)(b) to a person having control is a reference to a person having control in connection with the carrying on by him of a trade, business or other undertaking (whether for profit or not).

(5) The requirements imposed by these Regulations shall not apply to a person in respect of work equipment supplied by him by way of sale, agreement for sale or hire-purchase agreement.

(6) Subject to paragraphs (7) to (10), these Regulations shall not impose any obligation in relation to a ship's work equipment (whether that equipment is used on or off the ship).

Note on the text: the words 'relevant self-employed person' in paragraph (3)(a) are a later amendment (shown as F1 on the revised text) to the original words 'self-employed person'. That amendment affects only paragraph (3)(a). Paragraph (5) — the sale exclusion — is in its original 1998 wording and has not been amended. Paragraphs (7) to (10) concern ships' work equipment and are not material to a sale on land.

=====================================================================
4. ANALYSIS OF THE SALE EXCLUSION, ELEMENT BY ELEMENT
=====================================================================

'THE REQUIREMENTS IMPOSED BY THESE REGULATIONS SHALL NOT APPLY'
This is a full disapplication, not a partial one and not merely a defence. It removes every requirement in PUWER (regulations 4 to 35, including the 'suitable for purpose', maintenance, inspection, information/instruction/training and marking duties) as against the excluded person, in the excluded respect.

'TO A PERSON'
The exclusion is personal and capacity-specific. It is not a statement that the equipment is outside the Regulations; it is a statement that the seller is outside the duties in that capacity. The equipment remains 'work equipment' in the purchaser's hands and the purchaser's own duties under regulations 3(2) and 3(3) are untouched. HSE guidance makes the same point in terms: 'The Regulations do NOT apply to those who have supplied or sold equipment. It's up to the purchaser of equipment to make sure that it is specified, installed and used so that it does not present a risk to those at work.'

'IN RESPECT OF WORK EQUIPMENT SUPPLIED BY HIM'
The exclusion attaches to the supply act and the supplier's role in it. It does not travel with the equipment. It does not follow the distributor into an unrelated role at the purchaser's premises.

'BY WAY OF SALE, AGREEMENT FOR SALE OR HIRE-PURCHASE AGREEMENT'
This phrase is the operative limit, and it is narrower than the word 'supply' on its own:
  - 'Sale' — a completed sale, where property passes on or before delivery.
  - 'Agreement for sale' — a contract of sale under which property passes later (e.g. on payment in full, retention of title, conditional sale). This is inside the exclusion even though, at the moment of delivery, the seller may still hold title.
  - 'Hire-purchase agreement' — inside the exclusion, notwithstanding that the supplier retains title until the final instalment and the transaction has financing features.
  - NOT covered: ordinary hire, rental, leasing, loan, consignment stock, sale-or-return pending acceptance, or supply with an operator. These are supplies, but they are not sale, agreement for sale or hire-purchase, so the exclusion in regulation 3(5) does not bite. A supplier who hires out equipment can be a person 'having control' of it under regulation 3(3)(b) and is then within PUWER to the extent of that control. HSE's own overview describes PUWER as reaching businesses 'involved in providing work equipment for others to use (eg for hire)'.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE DISTRIBUTOR
The distributor, acting only as seller, is outside PUWER. It does not owe the PUWER duties to the purchaser or to the purchaser's employees. Those duties sit with the purchaser as employer (regulation 3(2)) and with anyone who has control of the equipment or of its use at the purchaser's premises (regulation 3(3)(b)).

=====================================================================
5. SUPPORTING GUIDANCE (consistent with the statutory text)
=====================================================================
- HSE priced guidance on PUWER: 'The Regulations do NOT apply to those who have supplied or sold equipment. It's up to the purchaser of equipment to make sure that it is specified, installed and used so that it does not present a risk to those at work.'
- HSE L22 (Fourth edition, 2014), ACOP and guidance: 'The Regulations, commonly known as PUWER, place duties on people and companies who own, operate or have control over work equipment. PUWER also places responsibilities on businesses and organisations whose employees use work equipment, whether owned by them or not.'
- HSE PUWER overview: duties fall on those who 'own, operate or have control over work equipment', and on businesses 'involved in providing work equipment for others to use (eg for hire)'.
- HSE L22 reproduces regulation 3 with paragraph (5) in the same words quoted in section 3.

=====================================================================
6. WHAT THE EXCLUSION DOES NOT DO — FOUR WAYS A DISTRIBUTOR CAN STILL BE IN SCOPE
=====================================================================
A distributor that sells equipment is not thereby immune from PUWER. The exclusion operates only on the sale. Each of the following is a separate basis of duty and should be checked against the distributor's actual operations:

(i) EMPLOYER CAPACITY (regulation 3(2)). The distributor is an employer. Any work equipment it provides for use by its own employees — warehouse forklifts, pallet trucks, ladders, hand tools, demonstration units, pressure washers, compressors, vehicle lifts, workshop equipment — is fully within PUWER, with all the regulation 4–35 duties (suitability, maintenance, inspection, guarding, information, instruction, training, marking).

(ii) RELEVANT SELF-EMPLOYED PERSON (regulation 3(3)(a)). A sole-trader distributor who uses work equipment at work is within scope in that capacity.

(iii) PERSON HAVING CONTROL (regulation 3(3)(b)). To the extent of its control, PUWER applies to a person who controls the equipment, controls a person who uses/supervises/manages its use, or controls the way it is used. Risk areas for a distributor: a demonstration or hire fleet; installation, commissioning or setting-up at the customer's site; retained servicing, maintenance or inspection obligations; equipment placed on consignment or sale-or-return in a customer's premises; retained rights to enter, inspect, modify or decommission. A distribution agreement that reserves such rights is evidence of control and should be reviewed.

(iv) NON-SALE SUPPLY. As set out in section 4, hire, rental, leasing and loan are outside regulation 3(5). A distributor with any rental or lease line of business is a potential regulation 3(3)(b) duty holder for that equipment.

=====================================================================
7. WHAT APPLIES TO THE DISTRIBUTOR INSTEAD (outside PUWER — flagged, to be verified separately)
=====================================================================
The sale exclusion in regulation 3(5) is not a statement that the distributor has no health and safety obligations at all. The following regimes are outside the scope of this opinion and must be checked separately before the distributor treats itself as clear:
- Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, section 6 — duties on designers, manufacturers, importers and suppliers of articles for use at work (safe design and construction, testing, adequate information, revision of information). This is the principal route by which supply-side duties reach a distributor, and it is not displaced by PUWER regulation 3(5).
- Product supply law for machinery in Great Britain. HSE's PUWER overview states that when providing new work equipment for use at work the provider must ensure conformity with the essential requirements of relevant product supply law — for new machinery, the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations — and must check conformity marking, manufacturer's details, Declaration of Conformity, instructions in English, and freedom from obvious defects. The version of that instrument in force on 2026-11-21 must be confirmed before it is cited.
- Any sector-specific supply regime applicable to the particular equipment.

=====================================================================
8. VERSION AND CURRENCY RECORD FOR 2026-11-21
=====================================================================
Instrument: Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998, SI 1998/2306. Citation and commencement: regulation 1 — in force 5 December 1998.

Verification chain for regulation 3(5):
1. Current revised text, legislation.gov.uk body view, fetched 2026-11-23T00:07:02Z (sha256 b6d195f8b158...). Page carries: 'There are currently no known outstanding effects for The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998.' Regulation 3(5) appears in the form quoted in section 3.
2. Point-in-time version at 2013-07-01, legislation.gov.uk (sha256 bbd05a874229...). Regulation 3(5) appears in identical words.
3. HSE priced guidance on PUWER (sha256 06914cc354f3...). Regulation 3(5) appears in identical words; guidance text states the Regulations do not apply to those who have supplied or sold equipment.
4. HSE L22, Safe use of work equipment, Fourth edition 2014 (sha256 e724bb336efd...). Regulation 3(5) appears in identical words.

Conclusion on currency: the sale exclusion in regulation 3(5) has been textually stable from 1998 to the latest revised text and is unaffected by the only amendment visible in regulation 3 (the 'relevant self-employed person' change in paragraph (3)(a)). No amendment to regulation 3(5) was identified that would be in force on 2026-11-21.

Residual limitation, stated honestly: the current text was fetched on 2026-11-23, two days after the stated date of 2026-11-21. The position 'as in force on 2026-11-21' is therefore inferred from the latest revised text plus the 'no known outstanding effects' statement, not read directly from a point-in-time snapshot of that exact date. Before relying on this in a contested matter, pull the legislation.gov.uk point-in-time view for 2026-11-21 and re-confirm regulation 3(5) verbatim. The conclusion is very unlikely to change, because a change would require an amending instrument affecting regulation 3(5) made and in force within that two-day window.

=====================================================================
9. PRACTICAL ACTIONS FOR THE DISTRIBUTOR (record these)
=====================================================================
1. Classify each transaction: sale / agreement for sale / hire-purchase (excluded by regulation 3(5)) versus hire, rental, lease, loan or consignment (NOT excluded). Record the classification per contract, not per customer.
2. Where any transaction is hire/rental/lease/loan/consignment, or where the distributor installs, commissions, services, maintains, inspects or retains rights to enter or modify, carry out a written regulation 3(3)(b) control assessment and record the extent of control and the resulting duties.
3. Confirm and document the employer-side PUWER compliance for the distributor's own staff and premises (equipment register, suitability, maintenance, inspection regime, training, information and instruction).
4. Keep the sale exclusion evidenced: the contract of sale or hire-purchase agreement, delivery documentation and invoice terms, so the capacity is demonstrable.
5. Do NOT extend the regulation 3(5) reasoning to product-safety obligations. Run the section 7 checks separately.
6. If the distributor operates in Northern Ireland, re-run this opinion against SR 1998/279.

=====================================================================
10. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER
=====================================================================
- The distributor is in Northern Ireland (different instrument; unverified here).
- The transaction is hire, rental, lease, loan or consignment rather than sale, agreement for sale or hire-purchase.
- The distributor retains control of the equipment, of a person using it, or of the way it is used, at the purchaser's premises.
- The distributor is an employer whose employees use the equipment, or a relevant self-employed person using it at work.
- An amendment to regulation 3(5) in force on 2026-11-21 — none identified, and the point-in-time re-check in section 8 should close this off.

=====================================================================
11. LIMITS OF THIS OPINION
=====================================================================
This opinion covers only the question asked: whether PUWER 1998, as in force on 2026-11-21, applies to a distributor in respect of equipment supplied by sale, and what the scope clause says on that point. It is given for Great Britain on the stated assumptions and does not address Northern Ireland, product supply law, HSWA section 6, contractual allocation of risk, or the position of the purchaser.

(2) Where engineering controls are provided to meet the requirements of regulation 7, the employer shall ensure that thorough examination and testing of those controls is carried out—

quotes.whole:
(2) Where engineering controls are provided to meet the requirements of regulation 7, the employer shall ensure that thorough examination and testing of those controls is carried out—
(a)in the case of local exhaust ventilation plant, at least once every 14 months, or for local exhaust ventilation plant used in conjunction with a process specified in Column 1 of Schedule 4, at not more than the interval specified in the corresponding entry in Column 2 of that Schedule; or
(b)in any other case, at suitable intervals.
(3) Where respiratory protective equipment (other than disposable respiratory protective equipment) is provided to meet the requirements of regulation 7, the employer shall ensure that thorough examination and, where appropriate, testing of that equipment is carried out at suitable intervals.
(4) Every employer shall keep a suitable record of the examinations and tests carried out in accordance with paragraphs (2) and (3) and of repairs carried out as a result of those examinations and tests, and that record or a suitable summary thereof shall be kept available for at least 5 years from the date on which it was made.

verdict.summary:
## Answer

Under the Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 (SI 2002/2677), as in force on 2026-11-21, the suitable record of examinations and tests of local exhaust ventilation (LEV) plant, and of repairs carried out as a result of those examinations and tests — or a suitable summary of that record — must be kept available **for at least 5 years from the date on which it was made**.

- Statutory minimum: **5 years** (a floor, not a target; longer retention is lawful and may be required by other regimes or by company policy).
- The clock runs from **the date on which the record was made**, not from the date of the examination if different, and not from the date the plant is decommissioned.

## Authority and exact text

Regulation 9 ("Maintenance, examination and testing of control measures"), paragraph (4), COSHH 2002, geographical extent E+W+S:

> "(4) Every employer shall keep a suitable record of the examinations and tests carried out in accordance with paragraphs (2) and (3) and of repairs carried out as a result of those examinations and tests, and that record or a suitable summary thereof shall be kept available for at least 5 years from the date on which it was made."

Paragraph (2)(a) is the provision that puts LEV plant within paragraph (4): thorough examination and testing of LEV plant at least once every 14 months, or at the shorter interval in Column 2 of Schedule 4 where the LEV serves a process listed in Column 1 of that Schedule. Paragraph (3) brings non-disposable respiratory protective equipment into the same record-keeping duty. Paragraph (4) therefore covers LEV records, RPE examination records, and the repairs arising from either.

## Point-in-time confirmation (the "as in force on 2026-11-21" constraint)

The retention period is stable across every version of the instrument, so the answer does not turn on which consolidation is used:

| Version | Reg 9(4) retention | 
|---|---|
| Original as made (made 24.10.2002; in force 21.11.2002) | at least 5 years from the date on which it was made |
| Point-in-time view at 2002-11-21 (legislation.gov.uk, /uksi/2002/2677/regulation/9/2002-11-21) | at least 5 years from the date on which it was made |
| Latest revised version (legislation.gov.uk, /uksi/2002/2677/regulation/9) | at least 5 years from the date on which it was made |
| HSE ACOP L5 (Control of substances hazardous to health), reg 9 quoted text | at least 5 years from the date on which it was made |

The only amendment ever made to regulation 9 is textual amendment F1, which substituted paragraph (1) with effect from 6 April 2005 (SI 2004/3386, reg. 2(e)). The legislation.gov.uk page for section 9 states: "There are currently no known outstanding effects for The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002, Section 9." Paragraph (4) has not been amended since it was made. Accordingly, any instrument in force on 2026-11-21 that purported to change the retention period would have had to appear as a textual amendment to reg 9(4); none is recorded. The figure of 5 years is therefore correct for 2026-11-21 on the text available.

## What the duty requires in practice

1. **Who.** "Every employer" who provides LEV plant (or non-disposable RPE) to meet reg 7. The duty is on the employer, not on the LEV examiner or contractor, although the employer may hold the record via a contractor.
2. **What.** A "suitable record" of the thorough examination and test, and of repairs carried out as a result. A "suitable summary" may be kept available **instead of** the full record — the regulation expressly permits the summary route.
3. **How long.** At least 5 years from the date the record was made. Diarise disposal no earlier than the fifth anniversary; do not destroy on plant replacement, site closure or contract change while the 5-year window is open.
4. **"Kept available" — meaning.** The regulation does not define the place or the audience; it requires the record or summary to be retrievable and producible on request. In practice that means: retrievable within the timescale an HSE inspector or local authority inspector allows under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, s.20 (inspectors' power to require production of, and take copies of, records), and accessible to employees and safety representatives who have a legitimate interest in the control measures protecting them. Electronic retention satisfies the duty provided retrieval is reliable and the record is legible and complete.
5. **No cessation-of-trading transfer duty.** Unlike reg 10(7)(c) for exposure monitoring records (which requires the employer, on ceasing to trade, to notify HSE and make monitoring records available to it), reg 9 contains no equivalent provision for LEV records. The 5-year retention duty simply runs its course; good practice is nonetheless to offer records to HSE or to a successor undertaking on cessation.

## Content of a suitable record (good practice, drawn from HSE guidance, not from the regulation itself)

The regulation does not prescribe fields. A record that will withstand scrutiny typically captures: unique plant/asset identifier and location; date of examination and test; the examiner's name and evidence of competence; methods and instruments used; measured results against the original commissioning/design specification (e.g. transport velocities, static pressures, capture/face velocity, duct integrity, air cleaner condition, fan condition, discharge position); defects identified; repairs carried out, by whom and when; the date the plant was returned to effective service; and the next examination due date.

## Do not confuse these periods

| Record type | Provision | Retention |
|---|---|---|
| LEV / RPE examination, test and repair records (or summary) | COSHH reg 9(4) | **at least 5 years from the date the record was made** |
| LEV thorough examination and test **frequency** (not retention) | COSHH reg 9(2)(a) and Sch 4 | at least once every 14 months, or the Sch 4 interval |
| Exposure monitoring records representative of identifiable employees' personal exposure | COSHH reg 10(5)(a) | at least 40 years from the date of the last entry |
| Other exposure monitoring records | COSHH reg 10(5)(b) | at least 5 years from the date of the last entry |
| Health records | COSHH reg 11 | separate and longer requirement — outside the scope of this answer; read reg 11 directly before relying on a figure |

The 14-month examination interval and the 5-year retention period are frequently conflated in secondary summaries. They are different duties in different paragraphs of the same regulation.

## Jurisdictional note

COSHH 2002 extends to England, Wales and Scotland (E+W+S). Northern Ireland has a separate instrument (Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations (Northern Ireland)) and is not governed by SI 2002/2677; if the plant is in Northern Ireland, the equivalent NI provision must be checked rather than this one.

## Source cross-check supporting the figure

The wording "at least 5 years from the date on which it was made" was confirmed identically in five independent retrievals: legislation.gov.uk point-in-time view (21.11.2002), legislation.gov.uk latest revised view, the original made PDF of SI 2002/2677, the FAO-hosted copy of the 2002 instrument, and the HSE ACOP L5 text quoting reg 9.

verdict.summary:
SAFETY OFFICER'S DETERMINATION — RIDDOR 2013, over-seven-day injury: reporting deadline

=====================================================================
1. ANSWER (bottom line)
=====================================================================
Where a person at work is incapacitated for routine work for more than seven consecutive days (excluding the day of the accident) because of an injury resulting from a work accident, the responsible person must send the report to the relevant enforcing authority in an approved manner **as soon as practicable and in any event within 15 days of the accident**.

- Statutory basis: Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 2013 (SI 2013/1471), regulation 4(2).
- Outer limit: 15 calendar days, counted from the date of the accident.
- The 15-day figure is unchanged in the version in force on 2026-11-21 (see section 3).
- 'As soon as practicable' is a separate, earlier obligation that runs alongside the 15-day long-stop. Fifteen days is the outside limit, not a target.

=====================================================================
2. STATUTORY TEXT RELIED ON
=====================================================================
Regulation 4(2) (verbatim, point-in-time version at 06/04/2026):

  '(2) Where any person at work is incapacitated for routine work for more than
  seven consecutive days (excluding the day of the accident) because of an injury
  resulting from an accident arising out of or in connection with that work, the
  responsible person must send a report to the relevant enforcing authority in an
  approved manner as soon as practicable and in any event within 15 days of the
  accident.'

Regulation 4(3): 'This regulation is subject to regulations 14 and 15.' (Carve-outs for cases already covered by other statutory reporting regimes; they do not alter the 15-day period for the ordinary case described in the question.)

Definitions in regulation 2 relevant to the trigger:
- 'consecutive days' includes any days which are not or would not have been working days.
- 'routine work' means work which a person might reasonably be expected to do, either under that person's contract of employment or, if there is no such contract, in the normal course of that person's work.
- 'responsible person' means the person identified in accordance with regulation 3 (for an employee at work, the employer; for a self-employed person in premises under someone else's control, the person in control of the premises; and so on).

Related provisions that sit around the same event:
- Reg 12(1)(c): a record must be kept of any injury to a person at work incapacitating them for routine work for **more than three consecutive days** (excluding the day of the accident) — the 'over-three-day' record, which is not a report.
- Reg 12(2)-(3): records kept for at least **three years** from the date the entry was made, at the place of work or the responsible person's usual place of business; extracts supplied to the enforcing authority on request.
- The single-report provision in the reporting procedure: where more than one reporting requirement applies, one report suffices if the stated conditions are met; otherwise the shortest applicable time limit governs.

=====================================================================
3. VERSION CHECK — TEXT IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21
=====================================================================
- legislation.gov.uk 'Changes over time' for SI 2013/1471 lists amendment points at 01/10/2013, 01/10/2014, 06/04/2015, 19/07/2015, 01/10/2015, 16/10/2015, 06/04/2017, 01/01/2018, 09/04/2018 and **06/04/2026**. The latest available point-in-time version is 06/04/2026, with the note 'There are currently no known outstanding effects'.
- 2026-11-21 falls after 06/04/2026 and there is no later amendment point, so the 06/04/2026 point-in-time text is the text in force on the date asked about.
- Reg 4(2) in the 06/04/2026 version is word-for-word identical to reg 4(2) in the 06/04/2015 point-in-time version. The 2026 amendment therefore did not touch the over-seven-day reporting period or the seven-day threshold.
- Corroboration from a regulator's current guidance (ORR, 'Guidance on RIDDOR 2013 regulations', authored 30 July 2025), paras 2.3-2.5: report 'as soon as practicable and in any event within 15 days of the accident'; the day of the accident is not counted in the seven days; weekends, rest days and holidays are counted; 'more than seven consecutive days' means at least eight days.
- Caveat: legislation.gov.uk states that revised text may not be fully up to date. The conclusion here is robust to that caveat because both the 2015 and 2026 point-in-time texts carry the same 15-day wording.

=====================================================================
4. HOW THE DEADLINE IS COMPUTED
=====================================================================
Step 1 — Identify the accident date (day 0).
Step 2 — Count the seven-day test: exclude the day of the accident; count every subsequent calendar day, including days the person would not normally have worked (weekends, rest days, leave, holidays). The injury becomes an 'over-seven-day injury' once the incapacity has lasted **more than seven consecutive days, i.e. at least eight days** — earliest ascertainable on day 8 after the accident.
Step 3 — Compute the report deadline as 15 calendar days from the accident date (day of accident = day 0; deadline is the end of day 15). Calendar days, not working days; bank holidays do not extend it.
Step 4 — Submit in an approved manner (the form approved for the time being by HSE, or by ORR for rail/guided-transport activities) and, in any event, as soon as practicable — the earlier of the two obligations governs.

Worked example
  Accident: Monday 2 March 2026 (day 0).
  Day 1 = Tue 3 Mar; day 8 = Tue 10 Mar (earliest date on which the over-seven-day threshold can be established).
  Deadline: 17 March 2026 (2 Mar + 15 days).
  Practical window between certainty of reportability and the long-stop: 7 days (10 Mar to 17 Mar).

Second example (illustrating that non-working days count)
  Accident: Friday 6 November 2026. Days 1-2 = Sat 7/Sun 8 Nov (counted even though not working days). Day 8 = Sat 14 Nov. Deadline: 21 November 2026 (6 Nov + 15).

=====================================================================
5. DEADLINE TABLE — RIDDOR 2013 (for contrast and to prevent mis-application)
=====================================================================
| Event                                                        | Provision | Time limit |
|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----------|------------|
| Specified injury to a worker                                 | reg 4(1)  | As soon as practicable (reporting procedure) |
| Over-seven-day injury to a worker                            | reg 4(2)  | As soon as practicable and in any event **within 15 days of the accident** |
| Non-fatal injury to a non-worker (hospital treatment etc.)   | reg 5     | Reporting procedure (as soon as practicable) |
| Work-related fatality                                        | reg 6     | Reporting procedure; written report within 10 days |
| Dangerous occurrence                                         | reg 7     | Within 10 days (10 working days for the offshore sub-category) |
| Over-three-day injury (record only, not reportable)          | reg 12(1)(c) | Record made; kept 3 years |

=====================================================================
6. EDGE CASES AND INTERPRETIVE POINTS THE RESPONSIBLE PERSON SHOULD KNOW
=====================================================================
(a) 'As soon as practicable' bites first. The 15 days is a long-stop. If the over-seven-day threshold is crossed on day 8, the expectation is a report promptly thereafter; waiting until day 15 without reason is inconsistent with the duty.
(b) The 15-day clock runs from the accident, not from the day the threshold is crossed. The statutory language is 'within 15 days of the accident'. Because reportability is only certain on day 8, the effective working window is roughly seven days.
(c) Late-appearing incapacity. Where the injury initially appears minor and the incapacity only later extends beyond seven days, the statutory outer limit is still 15 days from the accident; in practice a report made promptly once the threshold is crossed is what the 'as soon as practicable' limb requires. Treat this as regulator practice, not as an extension of the text.
(d) Counting. Days the person would not normally have worked are counted. 'Routine work' covers the full range of normal duties, not just attendance — a person on light duties who cannot do their normal job is incapacitated for routine work.
(e) Record separately. Even where the injury never reaches eight days, an over-three-day incapacity must be recorded under reg 12(1)(c) and the record kept for at least three years.
(f) Single report. If the same accident also triggers another reporting requirement (e.g. a specified injury under reg 4(1) or a fatality under reg 6), one report may serve, but the shortest applicable time limit must be met — which in practice means reporting immediately and not waiting for day 15.
(g) Regulations 14 and 15 (applied by reg 4(3)) restrict reporting where the incident is already covered by another statutory reporting regime. Where they apply, the reg 4(2) duty is displaced; where they do not, the 15-day period applies unchanged.
(h) Territorial scope. RIDDOR 2013 extends to England, Wales and Scotland. Northern Ireland has its own regulations; do not apply the 15-day figure there without checking the NI instrument.
(i) Enforcing authority. 'Relevant enforcing authority' is HSE or the local authority in most premises; ORR for activities within the Health and Safety (Enforcing Authority for Railways and Other Guided Transport Systems) Regulations 2006. The identity of the authority does not change the 15-day period; the 'approved manner' (form) differs.

=====================================================================
7. OPERATIONAL PROCEDURE (what the responsible person actually does)
=====================================================================
1. On the day of the accident, open an incident record: date, time, injured person, injury, whether a specified injury, whether the person is likely to be absent from routine work.
2. If a specified injury is present, report immediately under reg 4(1) — do not wait for the seven-day question to resolve.
3. Diarise day 8 from the accident date. On day 8, confirm whether the person has been incapacitated for routine work for more than seven consecutive days (counting non-working days, excluding the day of the accident).
4. If yes: submit the over-seven-day report in the approved manner immediately (online form for HSE-enforced premises; ORR's approved route for rail/guided transport).
5. Record the submission date/time and retain a copy. Confirm submission is on or before day 15 from the accident; if the long-stop is at risk, escalate and submit what is available — a prompt incomplete report is better than a late one.
6. Open/keep the reg 12 record (including the over-three-day entry if applicable) for at least three years.
7. If the person subsequently dies within one year as a result of the accident, a fatality report under reg 6 is triggered separately — the over-seven-day report does not discharge it.

=====================================================================
8. ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITS OF THIS DETERMINATION
=====================================================================
- Assumes the incident is in Great Britain and not within a reg 14/15 carve-out.
- Assumes the standard employer/responsible-person duty applies (regulation 3).
- The statutory quotation is taken from the 06/04/2026 point-in-time version of SI 2013/1471, which is the version in force on 2026-11-21 on the publisher's timeline; the publisher's general caveat about currency is noted and does not affect the conclusion, since the 2015 and 2026 texts are identical on this point.
- Nothing here varies the answer: **15 days from the accident, and in any event as soon as practicable.**

verdict.summary:
GAGE MEASUREMENT LOCATION AND MEASUREMENT PLANE — 49 CFR PART 213 (in force 2026-11-21)

1. GOVERNING PROVISION
49 CFR § 213.53(a) — Gage (Subpart C, Track Geometry). Verbatim text, as it appears in both the eCFR current text and the CFR 2025 annual edition (revision date 2025-10-01):

  "(a) Gage is measured between the heads of the rails at right-angles to the rails in a plane five-eighths of an inch below the top of the rail head."

The identical sentence is repeated verbatim at § 213.323(a) for Class 6, 7, 8 and 9 track (Subpart G). The same 5/8 in reference plane is carried into the frog guard-face gage footnotes at §§ 213.143 and 213.355 ("A line five-eighths of an inch below the top of the center line of the head of the running rail, or corresponding location of the tread portion of the track structure") and into the alinement chord definition at § 213.327 ("The ends of the chord shall be at points on the gage side of the outer rail, five-eighths of an inch below the top of the railhead").

2. WHERE GAGE IS MEASURED (ASK 2)
Gage is the transverse clear distance between the two rail heads, measured from the gage line of one rail to the gage line of the other — i.e., from the gage-side face of one rail head (the side facing track center) to the gage-side face of the opposite rail head. The measurement is taken at right angles to the rails (perpendicular to the longitudinal axis of the rail at the point of measurement), not at right angles to the track centerline on curves, and not along the top surface of the rail.

In practice: the gage bar's two contact faces bear on the gage side of each rail head at the specified elevation, and the reading is the distance between those two gage lines. "Between the heads of the rails" excludes any measurement taken across the base/flange, across the field side, or across the running surface at the top of rail.

3. MEASUREMENT PLANE — DEPTH BELOW TOP OF RAIL HEAD (ASK 3)
The measurement plane is five-eighths of an inch below the top of the rail head:

  5/8 in = 0.625 in = 15.875 mm  (0.625 in x 25.4 mm/in)

Stated as a depth: 0.625 in (15.875 mm) vertically below the top of the rail head, on each rail, on both sides of the track. The offset is measured downward from the top of the rail head (top of rail / running surface) at the location of the measurement. It is a fixed, dimensioned offset prescribed by the rule — it is not derived from rail section, head width, or wear, and it is not scaled or adjusted for rail size.

Why the rule uses this plane: the rail head is not a sharp-edged rectangle; the head has a crown and a fillet radius at the gauge corner. A measurement taken at the top of rail is unstable and varies with head wear and with where on the crown the gauge contacts. Measuring 5/8 in down places the contact below the crown and below the gauge-corner fillet, on the near-vertical gauge face, giving a repeatable, wear-tolerant reference.

4. CLASS APPLICABILITY — SAME CONVENTION, DIFFERENT LIMITS
This is a measurement convention, so it is uniform across all track classes in Part 213: excepted track and Classes 1-5 (§ 213.53(a)) and Classes 6-9 (§ 213.323(a)) all use the same "between the heads of the rails, at right angles to the rails, in a plane 5/8 in below the top of the rail head" definition. Only the numeric gage LIMITS change with class (§ 213.53(b), § 213.323(b)):

  Excepted track     —  no minimum;  max 4 ft 10-1/4 in
  Class 1            —  min 4 ft 8 in; max 4 ft 10 in
  Class 2 and 3      —  min 4 ft 8 in; max 4 ft 9-3/4 in
  Class 4 and 5      —  min 4 ft 8 in; max 4 ft 9-1/2 in
  Class 6            —  min 4 ft 8 in; max 4 ft 9-1/4 in; max change of gage within 31 ft 3/4 in
  Class 7, 8         —  min 4 ft 8 in; max 4 ft 9-1/4 in; max change of gage within 31 ft 1/2 in
  Class 9            —  min 4 ft 8-1/4 in; max 4 ft 9-1/4 in; max change of gage within 31 ft 1/2 in

Those figures are transverse limits in feet-inches; they are dimensionally distinct from, and must not be confused with, the 0.625 in (5/8 in) vertical depth of the measurement plane. Nominal standard gage, 4 ft 8-1/2 in (56.5 in; 1435 mm), is also a transverse dimension measured at that same 5/8 in plane — it is not a separate measurement convention.

5. DATE-OF-FORCE DETERMINATION (ASK 1)
Applicability: Part 213 applies to "all standard gage track in the general railroad system of transportation" (§ 213.3(a)), with the exclusions in § 213.3(b) (e.g., plant railroad track not part of the general system). The measurement rule quoted above is the one that governs that track.

Text verification for 2026-11-21:
  (a) eCFR current text of § 213.53, fetched 2026-11-23 (two days after the target date), shows the quoted 5/8 in language — sha256 c2bbfde68769.
  (b) CFR 2025 annual edition, Title 49 vol. 4, part 213 (revision date 2025-10-01), § 213.53(a), shows the identical sentence — sha256 dc44ad94cf3f (PDF) / 257a5a2da36c (§ 213.53 XML).
  (c) § 213.323(a) XML from the CFR 2024 edition (rev. 2024-10-01) carries the identical sentence — sha256 95678a12aaa9.

Three separate vintages (2024 annual, 2025 annual, current-as-of-2026-11-23) all carry the same text. Because the source fetched after the target date shows no change, the text in force on 2026-11-21 is the quoted text; the only residual gap would be an amendment with an effective date of 2026-11-22 or 2026-11-23, which could not alter the rule in force on 2026-11-21 absent retroactive effect. § 213.53 carries no recent amendment note beyond its base text in the 2025 edition, and the last amendment note on the parallel Class 6-9 provision is 78 FR 16104 (Mar. 13, 2013), confirming long-term stability of this definition. Residual-risk closure step if a certified date-stamped copy is required: pull the eCFR point-in-time view for 2026-11-21 (Title 49, Part 213, § 213.53) and run a Federal Register search for documents amending "213.53" with effective dates in 2025-10-01 through 2026-11-21.

6. DISTINCTIONS TO AVOID IN APPLICATION
  - Gage vs. crosslevel/surface/warp/alinement: those are separate Subpart C requirements with their own conventions (§§ 213.327, 213.331, 213.332). The 5/8 in plane is the gage-measurement convention; alinement independently references the same 5/8 in plane for chord endpoints on the gage side of the outer rail, but the two measurements answer different questions.
  - Gage vs. frog guard-face gage: §§ 213.143 and 213.355 set guard check and guard face gage limits using a line 5/8 in below the top of the center line of the head of the running rail — same reference elevation, different quantity.
  - Top-of-rail crown vs. the 5/8 in plane: on head-worn or hollow-worn rail, "top of the rail head" is taken at the running surface at the measurement location; the 0.625 in offset is applied from that surface, not from an unworn profile or from the rail's original catalog height.

7. ONE-LINE ANSWER
Under 49 CFR 213.53(a) (and identically 213.323(a) for Classes 6-9), as in force on 2026-11-21, gage is measured between the heads of the rails — gage line to gage line — at right angles to the rails, in a plane 5/8 inch (0.625 in; 15.875 mm) below the top of the rail head.

§ 213.59
Elevation of curved track; runoff.
(a) If a curve is elevated, the full elevation shall be provided throughout the curve, unless physical conditions do not permit. quotes.whole:
TRACK SAFETY STANDARDS
Subpart A—General
§ 213.1
Scope of part.
(a) This part prescribes minimum safety requirements for railroad track that is part of the general railroad system of transportation. In general, the requirements prescribed in this part apply to specific track conditions existing in isolation. Therefore, a combination of track conditions, none of which individually amounts to a deviation from the requirements in this part, may require remedial action to provide for safe operations over that track. This part does not restrict a railroad from adopting and enforcing additional or more stringent requirements not inconsistent with this part.
(b) Subparts A through F apply to track Classes 1 through 5. Subpart G and 213.2, 213.3, 213.15, and 213.240 apply to track over which trains are operated at speeds in excess of those permitted over Class 5 track.

verdict.summary:
# Determination — curved-track requirements and a 0.20° curve under 49 CFR Part 213

## 1. Answer

**No.** Under 49 CFR Part 213 as in force on 2026-11-21, the requirements specified for curved track **do not apply** to a curve of 0.20 degree. A 0.20° curve falls below the curvature threshold in the part's applicability clause, so it is treated as non-curved (effectively tangent) for purposes of every requirement the part specifies *for curved track*.

## 2. Governing text (the scope clause that controls this question)

Subpart A — General, **§ 213.14 Application of requirements to curved track**:

> Unless otherwise provided in this part, requirements specified for curved track apply only to track having a curvature greater than 0.25 degree.
>
> [78 FR 16100, Mar. 13, 2013]

Identical rule for high-speed track, Subpart G, **§ 213.313 Application of requirements to curved track**:

> Unless otherwise provided in this part, requirements specified for curved track apply only to track having a curvature greater than 0.25 degree.
>
> [78 FR 16104, Mar. 13, 2013]

Both were confirmed word-for-word in the eCFR text of Part 213 and in the 2025 and 2024 annual CFR editions of Title 49, Volume 4. The source note in every instance is 78 FR 16100 / 16104 (Mar. 13, 2013), i.e. the provision has not been amended since 2013.

### 2.1 Why § 213.14 is "the scope clause" here, and not § 213.1 or § 213.3

The part has three layers of applicability, and the engineer's question is answered at the third:

| Clause | Function | Does it decide the 0.20° question? |
|---|---|---|
| § 213.1 Scope of part | Says the part prescribes minimum safety requirements for railroad track that is part of the general railroad system of transportation; Subparts A–F apply to Classes 1–5, Subpart G to higher speeds | No — establishes that the part governs at all, not which curvature-specific requirements attach |
| § 213.3 Application | Says the part applies to all standard gage track in the general railroad system, with listed exclusions | No — subject-matter jurisdiction, not curvature |
| **§ 213.14 (and § 213.313 for Subpart G)** | **"Application of requirements to curved track"** — states the curvature threshold at which curved-track requirements attach | **Yes — this is the operative clause** |

§ 213.14 is literally titled "Application of requirements to curved track" and its operative words — "Unless otherwise provided in this part…" — are the exact qualifier the engineer's question carries. The question is therefore answered on its own terms by reading the clause back to the engineer.

## 3. Applying the clause to 0.20 degree

The clause attaches curved-track requirements **only** where curvature is **greater than 0.25 degree**. That is a strict inequality with a hard floor.

- Curvature at issue: **0.20 degree**
- Regulatory threshold: **0.25 degree**
- Test: is 0.20 > 0.25? **No.**
- Result: the condition precedent in § 213.14 is not satisfied, so no requirement "specified for curved track" in Part 213 applies to this curve.

**Boundary note (safety-relevant, get it right in the field):** the clause excludes a curve of *exactly* 0.25 degree as well, because the threshold is "greater than," not "at least." A curve must be steeper than 0.25° before curved-track requirements attach. Do not round 0.25 up to "applies" and do not round 0.20 up to 0.25.

**Geometric cross-check (chord definition, R = 50 / sin(D/2)):**

- D = 0.20° → R ≈ 28,648 ft (≈ 5.43 miles)
- D = 0.25° → R ≈ 22,919 ft (≈ 4.34 miles)

The 0.20° curve has the larger radius, consistent with it being flatter than the 0.25° threshold curve. Using the arc definition (R = 5729.578 / D) gives R ≈ 28,648 ft at 0.20°, indistinguishable for this purpose; the choice of degree-of-curve convention does not change the conclusion.

## 4. What the "unless otherwise provided in this part" qualifier does — and does not — do

The qualifier preserves any provision elsewhere in Part 213 that either (a) extends curved-track requirements to gentler curves, or (b) states its own curvature rule. Reviewed against the part as in force:

| Provision | What it provides | Effect on a 0.20° curve |
|---|---|---|
| § 213.14 / § 213.313 | Curved-track requirements attach only above 0.25° | **Controls — requirements do not attach** |
| § 213.4 Excepted track | Operations may continue without complying with Subparts B, C, D and E unless otherwise expressly stated | Narrows applicability generally; does **not** extend curved-track requirements to gentler curves |
| § 213.17 Waivers | Administrator may waive requirements case-by-case | Relief mechanism, not an applicability rule; and a waiver cannot be assumed — a granted waiver must be produced |
| § 213.9(a) speed-limit exceptions (cross-references to §§ 213.57(b), 213.59(a), 213.113(a), 213.137(b) and (c)) | Modify maximum allowable operating speeds in specific circumstances | Speed provisions only; no curvature threshold of their own that reaches below 0.25° |
| § 213.57(b), § 213.59 | Elevation limits, elevation runoff, and curve speed formula | These **are** requirements "specified for curved track"; § 213.14 gates them out at 0.20° |
| Subpart G (§§ 213.301–213.369) | Parallel high-speed regime, with its own § 213.313 | Same 0.25° threshold; same result |

No provision surfaced in the part states a curvature threshold lower than 0.25 degree, and none expressly extends curved-track requirements to track flatter than 0.25 degree. The qualifier therefore does not displace the general rule for a 0.20° curve.

**Completeness step still owed before this is written into a compliance document:** run a full-text search of the current Part 213 for "degree," "curvature," and "curve" and confirm no section outside those reviewed above sets a different threshold. On the text available, the answer is not in doubt; this step closes the negative on the qualifier.

## 5. What still applies to track laid on a 0.20° curve — do not over-read the answer

The verdict is narrow. § 213.14 gates only requirements **"specified for curved track."** Requirements of general applicability continue to apply to the same track, because they are not conditioned on curvature:

- **Still applies:** gage (§ 213.53), track alinement (§ 213.55), track surface (§ 213.63) including the crosslevel/warp limits that are written for track generally, combined alinement and surface deviations (§ 213.65), track structure (Subpart D), inspection (Subpart F), and the class speed limits of § 213.9.
- **Does not attach by reason of curvature:** the curve-specific elevation ceiling (§ 213.57(a)), the curve speed formula of § 213.57(b), and elevation/runoff requirements of § 213.59.

**Caution on mixed provisions.** Some generally applicable sections contain curve-specific rows or paragraphs (for example, the crosslevel-on-curves row of the § 213.63(a) table, and the cant-deficiency tables of § 213.63(b)). Read each such provision as two provisions: the tangent/general limits apply; the curve-specific limits are gated by § 213.14 and do not attach to a 0.20° curve. Do not carry a curve-specific limit onto this track, and do not drop the general limit because the curve-specific one is inapplicable.

**Practical consequence.** At 0.20° (≈ 28,648 ft radius) the curve is operationally indistinguishable from tangent for the purposes of Part 213's curve provisions. Speed over this segment is governed by the class limits of § 213.9, not by a curve-derived posted speed under § 213.57(b).

## 6. Currency as of 2026-11-21

- The eCFR text of Part 213 retrieved 2026-11-23 (two days after the target date) carries § 213.14 and § 213.313 verbatim as quoted, with source notes 78 FR 16100 and 78 FR 16104 (Mar. 13, 2013).
- The CFR 2025 annual edition (Title 49, Vol. 4) and the CFR 2024 annual edition carry the identical text.
- No amendment to either section appears in the surfaced material between 2013 and the retrieval date.
- Residual window: a final rule effective on or before 2026-11-21 but published after the 2025 annual edition would appear in the 2026-11-23 eCFR text; it does not. A rule with an effective date between 2026-11-21 and 2026-11-23 would be immaterial to the target date.

Conclusion: the quoted text is the text in force on 2026-11-21.

## 7. Recommended record for the engineer (one-paragraph determination to file)

> Track segment [ID], curvature 0.20 degree measured by [method / chord length / date / instrument]. Under 49 CFR 213.14 (Subpart A), requirements specified for curved track apply only to track having a curvature greater than 0.25 degree; 0.20 degree is not greater than 0.25 degree. Accordingly, the curved-track requirements of Part 213 (including §§ 213.57 and 213.59 and the curve-specific limits within §§ 213.55 and 213.63) do not apply to this segment. Generally applicable requirements of Part 213 — gage, alinement, surface, track structure, inspection, and the § 213.9 class speed limits — remain in force. No provision of Part 213 has been identified that provides otherwise. Determined by [name], [title], [date].

**Safety caveat to carry forward:** § 213.1(a) states that the requirements apply to specific track conditions existing in isolation and that a combination of conditions, none of which individually is a deviation, may still require remedial action for safe operations. The § 213.14 determination removes curve-specific obligations only; it is not a finding that the segment needs no maintenance, and it does not shield the track owner from § 213.5 responsibility for compliance with the requirements that do apply.

quotes.whole:
(b) Cab passageways and compartments shall have adequate illumination.
§ 229.129
Locomotive horn.
(a) Each lead locomotive shall be equipped with a locomotive horn that produces a minimum sound level of 96 dB(A) and a maximum sound level of 110 dB(A) at 100 feet forward of the locomotive in its direction of travel. The locomotive horn shall be arranged so that it can be conveniently operated from the engineer's usual position during operation of the locomotive.

verdict.summary:
# Regulatory Determination — 49 CFR Part 229: Steam-Locomotive Scope and Lead-Locomotive Horn Sound Levels

Prepared by: Regulatory Specialist. Deliverable is a determination memo with verbatim regulatory text, applicability analysis, and a reproducible compliance-test procedure.

---

## 0. Bottom line

| Ask | Determination |
|---|---|
| **2 — Scope as to steam locomotives** | **Part 229 does not apply to steam locomotives.** 49 CFR 229.1 (Scope) states: "This part prescribes minimum Federal safety standards for all locomotives except those propelled by steam power." Steam-propelled locomotives are therefore outside Part 229 in its entirety — including 229.129 (Locomotive horn). Steam locomotives are regulated instead under 49 CFR Part 230 (Steam Locomotive Inspection and Maintenance Standards). |
| **3 — Lead-locomotive horn sound level at 100 ft forward** | **Minimum 96 dB(A); maximum 110 dB(A).** 49 CFR 229.129(a): "Each lead locomotive shall be equipped with a locomotive horn that produces a minimum sound level of 96 dB(A) and a maximum sound level of 110 dB(A) at 100 feet forward of the locomotive in its direction of travel." |

---

## 1. Version control (discharge of the "as in force on 2026-11-21" constraint)

**Governing text used.** The determination rests on the codified text of Part 229, not on secondary commentary. Three independent official artifacts were compared:

| Source | Nature | § 229.1 text | § 229.129(a) text |
|---|---|---|---|
| GovInfo, CFR 2021 title 49 vol. 4, part 229 (PDF) | Annual print edition, 2021 | — | "minimum sound level of 96 dB(A) and a maximum sound level of 110 dB(A) at 100 feet forward of the locomotive in its direction of travel" |
| GovInfo, CFR 2025 title 49 vol. 4, part 229 (XHTML/XML) | Annual print edition, 2025 | "This part prescribes minimum Federal safety standards for all locomotives except those propelled by steam power." | same 96/110 dB(A) at 100 ft forward |
| eCFR, title 49 part 229 and § 229.129 (current, fetched 2026-11-23T00:23:40–41Z; sha256 4cc89b1b9843 / 5bc1879970b9 / 720cbb25fbb5 / f8147d846700) | Continuously updated codification | (unchanged) | "minimum sound level of 96 dB(A) and a maximum sound level of 110 dB(A)" |

**Conclusion on version.** The two provisions that carry the answer — 229.1 and 229.129(a) — are **identical** in the 2021 print, the 2025 print, and the eCFR point-in-time snapshot retrieved 2026-11-23, i.e. two days *after* the requested 2026-11-21 effective date. Because the text is unchanged across a span that brackets 2026-11-21 on both sides (2025 print before, 2026-11-23 eCFR after), the 2026-11-21 text of these provisions is established with high confidence. No amendment to 229.129 altering the 96/110 dB(A) pair, and no amendment to 229.1 altering the steam exclusion, appears anywhere in the retrieved record.

**Residual caveat (stated, not blocking).** eCFR "current" is a live page; the strict evidentiary artifact for a specific past date is an eCFR point-in-time (date-pinned) query or the Federal Register issue for any amendment effective 2025-10-01 through 2026-11-21. Recommended one-step re-verification before any enforcement or design action: run `https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-21/title-49.xml?part=229` (or the eCFR "Go to date" control set to 2026-11-21) and confirm 229.1 and 229.129(a) read as quoted. This is a confirmation step, not an open question: nothing in the retrieved record suggests a change.

---

## 2. Ask 2 — Scope of Part 229 regarding steam locomotives

### 2.1 Controlling text (verbatim)

> **§ 229.1 Scope.**
> This part prescribes minimum Federal safety standards for all locomotives except those propelled by steam power.

> **§ 229.3 Applicability.**
> (a) Except as provided in paragraphs (b) through (e) of this section, this part applies to all standard gage railroads.

### 2.2 Analysis

1. **The exclusion is categorical and sits in the scope section itself.** § 229.1 is a subject-matter limitation on the whole part, not an equipment-specific exemption buried in a subpart. A locomotive "propelled by steam power" is outside Part 229 root and branch.
2. **§ 229.3 does not pull steam locomotives back in.** § 229.3 fixes the *railroad* universe (standard gage railroads) to which the part applies; it presupposes the part's subject matter as already delimited by § 229.1. A standard gage railroad operating steam locomotives is within § 229.3(a)'s railroad class, but its steam-propelled locomotives are still outside the part's substantive reach by operation of § 229.1. The two sections operate at different levels (who vs. what) and do not conflict.
3. **Consequence for the horn rule.** Because § 229.129 lives inside Part 229, the 96/110 dB(A) lead-locomotive horn requirement **does not apply to steam locomotives**. A steam locomotive is neither a "lead locomotive" for § 229.129(a) purposes nor subject to the § 229.129(b) test obligations (built on/after 2006, built before 2006, remanufactured, replacement horn) or the § 229.129(c) test protocol as a matter of federal mandate under this part.
4. **Do not confuse "steam generators" with "steam propulsion."** Part 229 Subpart C contains §§ 229.103–229.114 under the heading STEAM GENERATORS (safe working pressure/factor of safety; steam generator number; pressure gauge; safety valves; water-flow indicator; warning notice; steam generator inspections and tests). These regulate **steam generators mounted on locomotives** (e.g., for train-line steam/heat) — typically diesel-electric locomotives — and are **not** the steam-propulsion exclusion. § 229.1's "propelled by steam power" is about motive power, not about auxiliary steam-raising equipment. A steam-generator-equipped diesel locomotive remains fully within Part 229.
5. **Where steam locomotives are regulated.** The FRA's steam program is 49 CFR Part 230 (Steam Locomotive Inspection and Maintenance Standards). Nothing in this memo should be read as stating that steam locomotives are unregulated; they are regulated elsewhere in Title 49.
6. **Adjacent consequence worth flagging (outside Part 229).** 49 CFR Part 222 (Use of Locomotive Horns at Public Highway-Rail Grade Crossings) builds on the Part 229 horn standard; because Part 229 excludes steam propulsion, a steam locomotive's participation in horn-based crossing-warning regimes is a Part 222 question, not a Part 229 question. Confirm under Part 222 before relying on any crossing-warning assumption for steam operations.

### 2.3 Determination

**Part 229's scope excludes steam locomotives entirely** — § 229.1: "all locomotives except those propelled by steam power." Accordingly, no requirement of Part 229, including § 229.129, attaches to a steam-propelled locomotive.

---

## 3. Ask 3 — Minimum and maximum horn sound level, each lead locomotive, 100 ft forward

### 3.1 Controlling text (verbatim)

> **§ 229.129 Locomotive horn.**
> (a) Each lead locomotive shall be equipped with a locomotive horn that produces a minimum sound level of 96 dB(A) and a maximum sound level of 110 dB(A) at 100 feet forward of the locomotive in its direction of travel. The locomotive horn shall be arranged so that it can be conveniently operated from the engineer's usual position during operation of the locomotive.

Corroborating definition (same thresholds, same geometry):

> **§ 229.5 Definitions — Defective.**
> Defective means, for purposes of section 229.129 of this part, a locomotive equipped with an audible warning device that produces a maximum sound level in excess of 110 dB(A) and/or a minimum sound level below 96 dB(A), as measured 100 feet forward of the locomotive in the direction of travel.

> **§ 229.5 Definitions — dB(A).** dB(A) means the sound pressure level in decibels measured on the A-weighted scale.

### 3.2 The numbers, with units and inclusivity

| Parameter | Value | Unit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum sound level, lead locomotive horn | **96** | **dB(A)** | § 229.129(a) |
| Maximum sound level, lead locomotive horn | **110** | **dB(A)** | § 229.129(a) |
| Measurement distance/orientation | **100 ft forward of the locomotive, in its direction of travel** | ft | § 229.129(a), (c)(7) |

**Inclusivity.** Read with the § 229.5 definition of *Defective*, the band is closed: a horn is defective only if it produces a maximum **in excess of** 110 dB(A) **and/or** a minimum **below** 96 dB(A). A horn measuring exactly 96 or exactly 110 dB(A) is compliant. The permissible band is therefore **96 ≤ L ≤ 110 dB(A)**.

**Per-locomotive, not per-consist.** The duty runs to "each lead locomotive." In a consist, the requirement is satisfied by the horn on the locomotive that is lead/controlling for the movement in question; each locomotive that is placed in lead service must itself comply. There is no averaging across a consist and no substitution of a trailing unit's horn.

**Not to be confused with cab noise.** §§ 229.121 and Appendix H set in-cab noise limits (e.g., 85 dB(A) average static noise with an upper 99% confidence limit of 87 dB(A), and the 82/85 dB(A) alteration ceilings) and use an LAeq,30s metric at four cab positions. Those are **cab-noise** limits, not horn limits, and must not be reported as the horn answer. The horn standard is § 229.129 only.

### 3.3 Measurement protocol (the number is only meaningful with its method)

Any statement of 96/110 dB(A) is a statement about a measurement made this way (§ 229.129(c)):

1. **Instrumentation.** Sound level meter properly calibrated and, at minimum, compliant with **IEC 61672-1 (2002-05), Class 2** — § 229.129(c)(1). Acoustic calibrator at minimum compliant with **IEC 60942 (1997-11), Class 2** — § 229.129(c)(2).
2. **Manufacturer instructions.** Follow the manufacturer's instructions on mounting/orienting the microphone, observer positioning, and periodic factory recalibration — (c)(3).
3. **Windscreen and mounting.** Use a microphone windscreen and tripods or similar mountings that minimize interference with the sound being measured — (c)(4).
4. **Test site.** Free of large reflective structures — barriers, hills, billboards, tractor trailers or other large vehicles, locomotives or rail cars on adjacent tracks, bridges, buildings — **within 200 feet to the front and sides of the locomotive**. Locomotive positioned on **straight, level track** — (c)(5).
5. **Weather window.** Ambient air temperature **32 °F to 104 °F inclusive**; relative humidity **20% to 95% inclusive**; wind velocity **not more than 12 mph**; **no precipitation** — (c)(6).
6. **Microphone geometry** — (c)(7):
   - General (not cab-mounted or low-mounted): **100 ft forward of the front knuckle** of the locomotive, **15 ft above top of rail**, at an angle **no greater than 20° from the center line of the track**, oriented per the manufacturer's recommendations.
   - Cab-mounted or low-mounted horns: **100 ft forward of the front knuckle**, **4 ft above top of rail**, **≤20° from center line**, oriented per manufacturer's recommendations.
   - The observer **shall not stand between the microphone and the horn**.
7. **Background noise** — (c)(8): sound level at the test site immediately **before and after** each horn sounding event must be **at least 10 dB(A) below** the level measured during the horn sounding.
8. **Meter settings and calibration** — (c)(9): meter set for **A-weighting with slow exponential response**; calibrated with the acoustic calibrator **immediately before and after** compliance tests.

**Note on the request's phrasing vs. the rule's geometry.** The request's "100 feet forward" matches § 229.129(a)'s "100 feet forward of the locomotive in its direction of travel." The test protocol makes that precise: the reference point on the locomotive is the **front knuckle**, and the microphone height is 15 ft above top of rail (4 ft for cab-mounted/low-mounted horns). No substitution or reinterpretation of the request is required; report the figures as measured at that geometry.

### 3.4 Test obligations attached to the limits (§ 229.129(b))

These are the *when/whether-to-test* provisions, distinct from the limits themselves:

- **Built on or after 2006-09-18:** must be tested per § 229.129 to confirm compliance with (a); may instead be tested under an acceptance sampling scheme with probability ≤ .05 of rejecting a lot with a proportion of defectives equal to an AQL of 1% or less, as set forth in 7 CFR part 43 — (b)(1).
- **Built before 2006-09-18:** must be tested per § 229.129 **before 2010-06-24** — (b)(2).
- **Remanufactured locomotives** (as determined under § 229.5): must be tested per § 229.129 to confirm compliance with (a) — (b)(3).
- **Replacement horns:** must be tested per (c) before the next two annual tests required by § 229.27 are completed — (b)(4)(i); **exception** where the unit was already tested under (b)(1), (b)(2), or (b)(3) and the replacement horn is the **same model** with the **same mounting location and type of mounting** — (b)(4)(ii).

Movement of a non-complying locomotive is addressed separately by § 229.9 (Movement of non-complying locomotives).

### 3.5 Determination

For each lead locomotive within Part 229's scope, the horn must produce **a minimum of 96 dB(A) and a maximum of 110 dB(A) at 100 feet forward of the locomotive in its direction of travel** (§ 229.129(a); § 229.5 "Defective" confirms the same closed 96–110 dB(A) band and the same 100-ft-forward geometry).

---

## 4. Applying both answers together (the practical point)

The two asks interact: **because § 229.1 excludes locomotives propelled by steam power, the 96/110 dB(A) horn requirement of § 229.129(a) does not bind a steam locomotive.** Stating the horn numbers without the scope answer would be misleading for a steam operator, and stating the exclusion without the numbers would fail the request. The correct combined reading:

- **Diesel-electric, electric, and other non-steam-propelled lead locomotives:** horn must be **96–110 dB(A)** at 100 ft forward, tested per § 229.129(b)–(c).
- **Steam-propelled locomotives:** outside Part 229 by § 229.1; § 229.129 does not apply. Look to 49 CFR Part 230 for the governing federal steam-locomotive requirements, and to 49 CFR Part 222 for grade-crossing horn use.

---

## 5. Sources relied on

1. 49 CFR 229.1 (Scope) — GovInfo, CFR 2025 title 49 vol. 4, part 229 (XHTML, sha256 720cbb25fbb5); text: "all locomotives except those propelled by steam power."
2. 49 CFR 229.3 (Applicability) — same source.
3. 49 CFR 229.129 (Locomotive horn), paragraphs (a), (b)(1)–(4), (c)(1)–(9) — eCFR § 229.129 (sha256 5bc1879970b9); GovInfo CFR 2025 XML § 229.129 (sha256 f8147d846700); GovInfo CFR 2021 PDF (sha256 1ae768813654); eCFR part 229 (sha256 4cc89b1b9843).
4. 49 CFR 229.5 (Definitions: Defective; dB(A)) — eCFR part 229 (sha256 4cc89b1b9843); GovInfo CFR 2025 (sha256 720cbb25fbb5).
5. 49 CFR 229.121 and Appendix H (cab noise — cited only to distinguish, not as the horn answer).
6. 49 CFR 229.9 (Movement of non-complying locomotives); 49 CFR 229.27 (annual tests); 7 CFR part 43 (acceptance sampling).
7. Part 229 authority line: 49 U.S.C. 20103, 20107, 20133, 20137-38, 20143, 20168, 20701-03, 21301-02, 21304; 28 U.S.C. 2461 note; 49 CFR 1.89. Source: 45 FR 21109, Mar. 31, 1980, unless otherwise noted.
8. Adjacent: 49 CFR Part 230 (Steam Locomotive Inspection and Maintenance Standards); 49 CFR Part 222 (Use of Locomotive Horns at Public Highway-Rail Grade Crossings).

---

## 6. Statement of limits on this determination

- The determination is a reading of the codified regulatory text; it is not legal advice and does not waive any FRA interpretation or waiver (49 CFR Part 211) that may apply to a specific operation.
- Version verification for 2026-11-21 is by bracketing (2025 print before, 2026-11-23 eCFR after) plus text identity across 2021/2025/current; a date-pinned eCFR query for 2026-11-21 is the recommended confirming step (see § 1).
- Nothing here addresses state or local sound ordinances, which are separate from the federal locomotive-safety standard.

quotes.whole:
§ 73.21 Classes of AM broadcast channels and stations.




(a) Clear channel.  A clear channel is one on which stations are assigned to serve wide areas. These stations are protected from objectionable interference within their primary service areas and, depending on the class of station, their secondary service areas. Stations operating on these channels are classified as follows:




(1) Class A station.  A Class A station is an unlimited time station that operates on a clear channel and is designed to render primary and secondary service over an extended area and at relatively long distances from its transmitter. Its primary service area is protected from objectionable interference from other stations on the same and adjacent channels, and its secondary service area is protected from interference from other stations on the same channel. (See § 73.182). The operating power shall not be less than 10 kW nor more than 50 kW. (Also see § 73.25(a)).






(2) Class B station.  Class B stations are authorized to operate with a minimum power of 0.25 kW (or, if less than 0.25 kW, an equivalent RMS antenna field of at least 107.5 mV/m at 1 kilometer) and a maximum power of 50 kW, or 10 kW for stations that are authorized to operate in the 1605-1705 kHz band.






(3) Class D station.  A Class D station operates either daytime, limited time or unlimited time with nighttime power less than 0.25 kW and an equivalent RMS antenna field of less than 107.5 mV/m at 1 kilometer. Class D stations shall operate with daytime powers not less than 0.25 kW nor more than 50 kW. Nighttime operations of Class D stations are not afforded protection and must protect all Class A and Class B operations during nighttime hours. New Class D stations that had not been previously licensed as Class B will not be authorized.








(b) Regional Channel.  A regional channel is one on which Class B and Class D stations may operate and serve primarily a principal center of population and the rural area contiguous thereto.




Note:


Until the North American Regional Broadcasting Agreement (NARBA) is terminated with respect to the Bahama Islands and the Dominican Republic, radiation toward those countries from a Class B station may not exceed the level that would be produced by an omnidirectional antenna with a transmitted power of 5 kW, or such lower level as will comply with NARBA requirements for protection of stations in the Bahama Islands and the Dominican Republic against objectionable interference.








(c) Local channel.  A local channel is one on which stations operate unlimited time and serve primarily a community and the suburban and rural areas immediately contiguous thereto.



(1) Class C station.  A Class C station is a station operating on a local channel and is designed to render service only over a primary service area that may be reduced as a consequence of interference in accordance with § 73.182. The power shall not be less than 0.25 kW, nor more than 1 kW. Class C stations that are licensed to operate with 0.1 kW may continue to do so.





[56 FR 64856, Dec. 12, 1991, as amended at 81 FR 2759, Jan. 19, 2016]

Regional channels; Class B and Class D stations.
(a) The following frequencies are designated as regional channels and are assigned for use by Class B and Class D stations: 550, 560, 570, 580, 590, 600, 610, 620, 630, 790, 910, 920, 930, 950, 960, 970, 980, 1150, 1250, 1260, 1270, 1280, 1290, 1300, 1310, 1320, 1330, 1350, 1360, 1370, 1380, 1390, 1410, 1420, 1430, 1440, 1460, 1470, 1480, 1590, 1600, 1610, 1620, 1630, 1640, 1650, 1660, 1670, 1680, 1690, and 1700 kHz.
(b) Additionally, in Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands the frequencies 1230, 1240, 1340, 1400, 1450, and 1490 kHz are designated as Regional channels, and are assigned for use by Class B stations. Stations formerly licensed to these channels in those locations as Class C stations are redesignated as Class B stations.
[56 FR 64857, Dec. 12, 1991]
§ 73.27
Local channels; Class C stations.
Within the conterminous 48 states, the following frequencies are designated as local channels, and are assigned for use by Class C stations: 1230, 1240, 1340, 1400, 1450, and 1490 kHz.
[56 FR 64857, Dec. 12, 1991]
§ 73.28
Assignment of stations to channels.

quotes.text: The vertical plane radiation characteristics show the relative field being radiated at a given vertical angle, with respect to the horizontal plane. The vertical angle, represented as θ, is 0 degrees in the horizontal plane, and 90 degrees when perpendicular to the horizontal plane. The vertical plane radiation characteristic is referred to as f(θ). The generic formula for f(θ) is: f(θ) = E(θ)/E(O) where: E(θ) is the radiation from the tower at angle θ. E(O) is the radiation from the tower in the horizontal plane.

[47 FR 8587, Mar. 1, 1982]
§ 73.14 AM broadcast definitions.
AM broadcast band.   The band of frequencies extending from 535 to 1705 kHz.
AM broadcast channel.   The band of frequencies occupied by the carrier and the upper and lower sidebands of an AM broadcast signal with the carrier frequency at the center. Channels are designated by their assigned carrier frequencies. The 117 carrier frequencies assigned to AM broadcast stations begin at 540 kHz and progress in 10 kHz steps to 1700 kHz. (See § 73.21 for the classification of AM broadcast channels).
AM broadcast station.   A broadcast station licensed for the dissemination of radio communications intended to be received by the public and operated on a channel in the AM broadcast band.
Amplitude modulated stage.   The radio-frequency stage to which the modulator is coupled and in which the carrier wave is modulated in accordance with the system of amplitude modulation and the characteristics of the modulating wave.
Amplitude modulator stage.   The last amplifier stage of the modulating wave amplitude modulates a radio-frequency stage.
Antenna current.   The radio-frequency current in the antenna with no modulation.
